item.title: The Real Banking History Behind George Bailey’s Building and Loan in ‘It’s a Wonderful Life’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear structure, and cultural significance

Halfway through Itâs a Wonderful Life, which opened in New York on December 20, 1946, George Bailey comes back from his own wedding to find a crowd at the Bailey Brothers Building and Loan demanding to be paid.

George tries to explain that he doesnât keep their cash in a safe: âThe moneyâs not here,â he says, and âyour moneyâs in Joeâs house,â and in the Kennedy house, and in a hundred others. Tom wants his $242 in cash, and George gives him a slip of paper to sign and tells him heâll get his money in 60 days. When Tom balks, George reminds him, âthatâs what you agreed to when you bought your shares.â

It plays like a stall, but a Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond history of building and loans says the withdrawal process in that scene is accurate. This is the story of the business George was actually trying to run.

You Didnât Deposit, You Joined

The building and loan was originally modeled on British building societies. The first American one was the Oxford Provident Building Association, which opened in 1831 in Frankford, Pennsylvania (now part of Philadelphia), and it was founded by two English-born factory owners. Members joined by signing up for $500 shares and paying $3 a month for each share.

Then they would take turns borrowing from the pot, often by bidding against each other for the next loan. Nobody was a depositor: you were a part-owner, which is why George can say the money is in the neighborsâ houses with a straight face.

This was a mortgage that a factory worker could get. National banks were not allowed to make real estate loans at all, and state banks could demand up to 60 percent down on loans that ran five years or less. According to Price and Walterâs longer paper, bank mortgages in the 1920s averaged three years, while building and loan mortgages averaged 11 years, and 95 percent of them paid themselves off. By 1927 there were 12,804 building and loan associations with 11.3 million members, in a country of 119 million people.

Building and loan mortgages were different from the mortgages we know today. The classic type was a share accumulation loan. The borrower kept buying shares in the building and loan each month until the value of the shares plus their dividends equaled what he owed. That typically took about 12 years, though it could run longer or shorter depending on the dividend rate.

In a direct reduction loan, each payment cut the principal, and the borrower knew the payoff date on day one. Those existed by the 1880s, but most associations didnât switch to them until the mid-1930s, after the mortgage crisis showed borrowers how much risk the old contract had put on them.

Why the 60 Days Mattered

A depositor in a bank could walk in and take out his money at any time. Building and loan members owned shares in the association, and under plans that allowed early withdrawal at all, the association commonly got 30 or 60 days to pay the member. The Richmond Fed says that made building and loans more stable than banks in panics like the one in 1907.

Still, the number of building and loans fell from 12,342 in 1929 to 8,006 ten years later. The closures didnât come from runs: many associations had borrowed short-term from banks, the banks had failed, and real estate prices had fallen.

Herbert Hoover proposed a system of mortgage banks in late 1931, and the Federal Home Loan Bank Act became law on July 22, 1932. As Hoover later wrote, the loss of the old homestead had been played out a million times ânot because of the designing villain but because of a fault in our financial system.â Bedford Falls got its villain anyway.

The Home Ownersâ Loan Act of June 13, 1933, authorized the chartering of âFederal Savings and Loan Associations,â and even these werenât accepting deposits yet (the law said âNo deposits shall be acceptedâ). A year later, the National Housing Act created the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation to insure the savings of such institutions.

Through the 1930s and 1940s, the industryâs name changed from âbuilding and loanâ to âsavings and loan,â part of a post-Depression makeover that historian David Mason described to Marketplace, as the St. Louis Fed recounts.

Where the Building and Loans Went

By 1980, the almost 4,000 S&Ls with $600 billion in assets had fallen into the exact trap the 60-day rule was built to avoid, funding long fixed-rate mortgages with short-term deposits. When inflation and interest rates shot up in the late 1970s and early 1980s, depositors fled for better rates elsewhere and the mortgages on the S&Lsâ books lost value.

According to the Federal Reserveâs history of the crisis, the insurance fund had $6 billion in reserves in 1983, but paying off the insured depositors of the failed thrifts would have cost roughly $25 billion. So regulators let the insolvent âzombiesâ keep operating. In 1987 the insurer decided it would be cheaper to burn down a bankrupt Texas thriftâs unfinished condominiums than to try to sell them.

Congress abolished the insurer in 1989, and the cleanup agency closed 747 S&Ls at a cost to taxpayers of up to $124 billion.

As of June 30, 2025, there were 503 S&Ls left in the U.S., so if you want to run down Main Street screaming âMerry Christmas, you wonderful old Building and Loan,â you can still find one.

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-27 20:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: These ancient goddesses were obsessed with sex and war. Here's why
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, insightful analysis, and cultural context

These ancient goddesses were obsessed with sex and war.

Ronald Hutton explains why goddesses embodying the dual forces of sex and violence are found across the ancient world

Danny Bird: What first drew you to this idea that love and war goddesses are often the same figure? And when did you realise the pattern was widespread enough across the ancient world to deserve a book?

Ronald Hutton: It was a slow process. I think the catalyst was that, as a classicist, I’d always been fond of and known a great deal about Venus and Aphrodite. What set me on the path of joining the dots was a symposium on the Sumerian goddess Inanna, with her famous descent into the underworld. That meant getting to know Inanna very well, and in doing so I noticed striking similarities in both persona and myth with Venus and Aphrodite. I then realised there were stepping stones connecting them, in places like Cyprus and Syria. I saw a kind of domino effect, whereby Inanna, in many ways, helped shape the personae of the other goddesses, one by one.

At that point I thought the picture was complete – my dominoes had fallen as far as the far end of the Mediterranean. But then I noticed how similar Freyja was in the Norse sagas. And finally, it struck me that the Morrigan, the Celtic goddess of love and war up in Ireland, was the missing piece of the jigsaw. With that, my gallery was complete.

So in the book you explore the stories of Inanna, Aphrodite, Venus, Freyja and the Morrigan, as well as the Egyptian goddess Hathor. Do any other deities make the cut?

That’s pretty well the lot. You’ve only left out Anat and Athtart – better known by her Greek name, ‘Astarte’ – who are found in Syria. These fall under what we might call the ‘Levantine Enigma’. Even though we have some wonderful legends about them, we know so much less about these colourful Syrian goddesses.

The legends are not quite enough to establish their identity, largely because they were written on unbaked clay tablets, which tend to crumble. We’ve got all these tablets from one ancient site on the coast of Syria, Ras Shamra. And tantalisingly, just as a story is really getting going, the tablet cracks, and we lose a chunk, or sometimes everything. Some stories survive only as tiny fragments.

You’ve structured the book around ‘the Family’, who fit the love-and-war template neatly, and ‘the Outliers’, who only carry some traits. Why did the Outliers belong in this story?

They’re only outliers geographically, whereas ‘the family’ are goddesses of love and war who seem to me to be joined up genealogically. The older among them helped to give birth to the younger in this wave-like movement from east to west, beginning with Inanna and ending with Venus.

Freyja and the Morrigan are outliers geographically, because they’re way to the north and west, and yet they’re strikingly similar. They don’t just have a few characteristics in common, they share the lot.

The only real outlier is Hathor, the Egyptian goddess of love, the Egyptian Venus. I had to include her, otherwise practically every reviewer would ask: “What about Hathor?” So, I put in Hathor, regrettably, only to show that she doesn’t fit.

What made this pairing of love and violence in one divine feminine figure so compelling and enduring for ancient worshippers?

That’s the big question, isn’t it? There’s no definitive answer. The most obvious one hinges on the fact that ancient warfare was largely a whole set of single combats [a duel between two single combatants]. Both love and war – well, sex and war – involved dramatic conjunctions of human bodies, and also ecstatic experiences in which people underwent extreme physical and emotional reactions and lost control of themselves. They went into battle frenzy, or the ecstasy of lovemaking.

There’s something I learned as a historical re-enactor, particularly in the Civil War Re-enactment Society of the Sealed Knot, which is that the single-combat effect on the battlefield is rather like picking a partner. As the two opposing lines come together, you’re selecting the person approaching you, the one you’re going to fight, and it’s like a dance. And that’s exactly what the ancient people called it.

- Read more | Three thousand years ago, the ancient Greeks turned an even older civilisation into a monster

I want to follow up on something from the book: this notion, particularly around Aphrodite, that love was seen by the ancients almost as an illness or madness, a surrender of control. Can you say more?

Yes, the Greeks – at least the really ancient Greeks, down to the time of Alexander the Great – were really quite terrified of love. A lot of the Greek male ethos was about self-control: about achieving balance, calm, harmony, self-knowledge, getting a grip on things. And both aspects of love, the emotional and the physical, are largely about losing control. So, this terrier-like propensity of Aphrodite to shake human beings about, like a dog shaking a rat, really unsettled the ancient Greeks. And the oldest Greek poetry is full of this outpouring of woe about what a dreadful thing love is.

These goddesses wielded huge power in the divine realm, but their worshippers were often living in patriarchal societies. What does that gap tell us about divine femininity versus ancient women’s real-world status?

It tells us that there’s no relationship between the two in any civilisation at any time. Look at India until recently, which is festooned with some of the most gung-ho, savage goddesses on the planet, and yet where the position of women has usually been more downtrodden than in most other places on the planet. In fact, you could posit, probably wrongly, an equation whereby the more feisty, terrifying and domineering the goddesses in a culture, the more browbeaten the human women.

I wouldn’t like to propose that as a truth, but it does work for certain cultures.

Do you think these cults ultimately speak more to masculine aggression than feminine power?…

Source: HistoryExtra | Published: 2026-11-27 15:30 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The invention that changed reading forever (and it wasn’t the Kindle)
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, historical significance, and cultural impact

We live in a time of technological revolution. The past 50 years have birthed the personal computer, the smartphone, and now artificial intelligence. While each is a world-changing invention and still relatively young, none yet rivals the movable-type printing press.

Starting around 1440 in Mainz, Germany, Johannes Gutenberg’s invention enabled information to spread as never before. It cultivated ideas, seeded revolutions, and so much more. It also gave birth to a new industry: bookselling. Though it’s hard to imagine today — with overstuffed bookshelves decorating any toddler’s bedroom and little free libraries as fixtures on city streets — books were almost exclusively sold to society’s elite for hundreds of years.

“The range of available customers and books was much narrower than we are accustomed to today, partly because books were still expensive,” Andrew Pettegree, the Bishop Wardlaw Professor of History at the University of St. Andrews, writes in his recently published book, The Bookshop: A History of Bookselling from the Dawn of Print to the Twenty-First Century.

Social elites have traditionally been the first adopters of almost every new technology; books were no exception. Among Europe’s wealthy, books were treasures to be read and displayed. Ostentatious libraries in their homes served as status symbols. Booksellers arose to cater to that market.

And for four centuries, this status quo didn’t really change.

“It is only in the 19th century that book ownership became possible and ultimately habitual for large sections of the population,” Pettegree writes. The cost of paper, historically the great barrier to widespread book ownership, finally fell enough to make books relatively affordable. But a massive “earthquake” was still on the horizon …

The paperback unleashed

For centuries, hardcovers were the norm, and entrenched interests sought to keep it that way. Printers, publishers, and booksellers alike knew they could produce and sell far cheaper paperback versions of books, but they resisted. In the early 20th century, hardcovers could sell for 15 times the price of a paperback, with much higher margins. Booksellers also didn’t want to cut into the lucrative used-book market. They knew that paperbacks couldn’t survive for long, even fretting that the books wouldn’t endure handling by curious shoppers perusing stocked shelves.

Grateful for curious minds

This Thanksgiving, get 15% off Big Think membership and join a community of idea explorers. Use code BIGTHANKS15 at checkout. Valid on annual plans for new members only.

Silly though that seems to us today, Pettegree told Big Think that booksellers back then likely had a point: “Libraries wouldn’t take paperbacks because they’d have to be rebound so frequently. These were very fragile books.”

But complaints and constraints couldn’t keep innovation down forever. In the summer of 1935, Penguin Books in Britain launched the first major line of paperbacks, priced at a fraction of the cost of hardcovers. Pocket Books in the U.S. followed suit a few years later, charging a quarter per paperback (about $6 today).

It changed everything, Pettegree says. Lower costs attracted new customers, giving book buying a new lease on life. Readers who would have instead borrowed a book from a library now became owners. And in a world where television wouldn’t become mainstream for another two decades, paperbacks brought entertainment home to the masses. They were the era’s binge-worthy shows, and “they spread like wildfire.”

“You had all this new urban population. When they came out of the mills after working 15 hours, they didn’t want to be improved by going to the public library. They wanted to read something amusing or exciting,” Pettegree says.

Arriving just before World War II, paperbacks also swiftly circulated to the battlefields of Europe. As Pettegree relates, British troops had a big pocket in their trousers that soon came to be called a “Penguin pocket” because you could carry a Penguin paperback in it. Doubling as localized body armor, the books may have even saved lives by absorbing the impact of shrapnel or bullets.

E-books a relative flop

No other innovation in bookselling has yet to approach the success of the paperback. Especially, Pettegree says, not e-books.

Though founder Jeff Bezos, in his own words, made killing “analog” books Amazon’s business and predicted that the vast majority of books would be in electronic form, his aspirations here have undeniably fizzled thus far. The Kindle was released almost three decades ago, and e-books remain in the minority.

“Physical books still command more than 80% of the marketplace,” Pettegree tallied. “In the past years, sales of e-readers have stalled. Incredibly, analog reactionaries retain the upper hand. … The relative underperformance of the e-reader is a welcome reminder that a new technology, however well designed, will not have everything its own way.”

While Pettegree is by no means a Luddite, he cheers this outcome.

“My wife bought me a Kindle. She said you’re a historian of communication and you should give it a go,” he told Big Think. He did so dutifully, loading it up with 20 or so novels and reading them all. But he found the process to be a slog and didn’t enjoy it.

Where is his Kindle now?

“It’s in the municipal skip.” (For American readers, that’s the trash bin.)

The future of selling books

Though he tossed his e-reader and recognizes the company’s downsides, Pettegree still praises Amazon. On the whole, he said, the company has provided readers with vastly more access to books — at heavily discounted prices, no less. If this persists, he will remain a reluctant fan.

“I love browsing in a bookshop, but … you have the world’s books at your disposal,” he shared with Big Think.

Pettegree has taken some heat for his kind words toward the world’s largest company by revenue, particularly in his college town. “People say, ‘I can’t believe that you said nice things about Amazon!…

Source: Big Think | Published: 2026-11-27 15:30 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: From Gandhi to Gen Z: A Century of Protest
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, historical perspective, and cultural significance

Gen Z protests in India in July demanded the resignation of the Minister for Education following a string of student suicides. The deaths followed the cancellation of a medical training examination after its exam paper was leaked. After millions engaged in peaceful protests throughout the country, the minister eventually resigned.

After a brief hiatus, the protests regained momentum following news that the election commissioner, who oversees the independent body responsible for conducting elections at both central and state levels, was accused of deleting thousands of names of eligible voters from electoral lists on the basis of their religion. Some parties claim that this has affected the outcome of elections across the country in favor of the Hindutva groups currently in power.

While the increased level of participation in these protests may seem surprising after years of citizens tolerating an increasingly fascist state apparatus, India has a long history of peaceful protests to bring about change.

Mahatma Gandhi’s non-violent movements, which began 100 years ago, brought the mighty British Empire to heel. “Under the inspiring leadership of Gandhi, several movements were launched to pinpoint the urgency and need for granting independence to India,” writes Dalip Singh in his paper “Protest Movements in India,” published in The Indian Journal of Political Science in 1991. These movements took place in phases, including the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920–21, the Civil Disobedience Movement of 1930–31, the Individual Disobedience Movement of 1940, and the Quit India Movement of 1942–45. The underlying principle common to all these movements, however, was non-violence. Singh writes, “Even those followers of Gandhi who did not believe in non-violence as a creed, accepted it as a political expediency. From the above account one has to accept that hunger strike, bandh, gherao, dharna, etc. had gained the legitimacy of the people during the nationalist movement.”

More to Explore

Caught in Partition’s Violent Fray

This system, termed the “Gandhian system of protest” by retired professor Chaman Lal, was lauded in an article published in the Economic and Political Weekly in 2016. He wrote of a gathering of writers and activists on the eighty-sixth anniversary of the historic Dandi March to “raise their voice against growing communal aggression against innocent people, not only in India, but throughout the world.”

David H. Bayley, meanwhile, divides the systems of protest in India into two distinct categories in a 1969 paper published in Pacific Affairs titled “Public Protest and the Political Process in India,” calling them legal and illegal forms of protest. The illegal forms come in two varieties—violent and nonviolent. Satyagraha, or nonviolent civil disobedience, is a nonviolent but often illegal form of protest. Violent illegal protest refers primarily to riots, although it may include assassinations and coups d’état as well. Bayley explains the political motivation for such violence:: “The point to underscore is that one common variety of social violence in Modern India has an explicitly political motivation, and it stems from a desire to shape government policy.” This, however, also seems to be the case with recent nonviolent protests.

A major cause of protests in the 1990s and early 2000s was the privatization of India’s economy. Katrin Uba collected data for her 2008 paper “Labor Union Resistance to Economic Liberalization in India: What Can National and State Level Patterns of Protests against Privatization Tell Us?” published in Asian Survey. Her findings reveal

increased anti-privatization protests and an enlarged repertoire of labor movement mobilization approaches from 1991 to 2003… While unions organized few protests during the early 1990s, their mobilization intensified as successive central governments and their state-level counterparts accelerated the pace and scope of privatization… This study also shows that all major labor unions in India, regardless of their ideological leanings, took part in protests against privatization.

More recent mass protests include those following the 2012 gang rape in Delhi, which, for a variety of reasons outlined by Poulami Roychowdhury in her article “The Delhi Gang Rape: The Making of International Causes,” published in a 2013 issue of Feminist Studies, “provoked a mass media furore across the globe.”

Weekly Newsletter

"*" indicates required fields

In 2019–20, there was mass mobilization against the passing of the Citizenship Amendment Act, which sought to define citizenship on the basis of religion, and 2021–22 saw farmer protests against economic policies seen as favoring private enterprises over agricultural ones. Both drew large crowds, with social media and WhatsApp groups becoming an important source of information, assistance, and support. Madhavi Shivaprasad describes the experience in her paper “Protest and Performance: My Engagement with the Anti-CAA-NRC Protests in India,” published in the Journal of Feminist Studies in Religion in 2021. She wrote,

Students’ Instagram, Twitter, and Facebook accounts became temporary “responsible” digital fact-checking sites for news around the anti-CAA-NRC protests as local and national news channels became unreliable. These accounts began to be counted as dependable because they were being shared by and among other fellow protesters. I became actively involved on a daily basis in online mobilization and amplification of the voices of people at the various sit-ins and protest events being organized around the CAA-NRC through social media such as Facebook and Twitter.

This reliance on social media was taken a step further in the recent Gen Z protests organized by the satirically named political body known as the Cockroach Janata Party, during which independent news outlets on social media platforms were the only sources of news considered reliable.…

Source: JSTOR Daily | Published: 2026-11-27 14:37 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Liminal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, poignant storytelling, and cultural insight

It’s estimated that as many as 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers and civilians have lost a limb since Russia began its full-scale invasion in 2022. At the Protez Foundation in Oakdale, Minnesota, such patients are fitted with state-of-the-art prosthetics free of charge and are taught how to use their new limbs. However, as the stirring short documentary Liminal captures, the process is far more than just physical.

For the film, the director Brennan Vance profiled a group of Ukrainian soldiers who, injured on the front lines, came to Minnesota to recover far from the brutal war that had defined their lives for years. Yet, despite their life-altering injuries, most were still eager to continue fighting, especially as the US commitment to the cause seemed to be waning. With the encouraging guidance of Yakov Gradinar, the Ukrainian-American chief medical officer at the Protez Foundation, the young men learned not only how to be in their bodies once again, but also how to inhabit the world. Poignant and inspiring, Vance’s documentary is both a unique window into the ongoing conflict and a powerful portrait of what it means to suffer a profound loss and yet still find a way forward.

item.title: The energy of thought
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, thought-provoking analysis, and cultural relevance

Listen to this essay

20 minute listen

Making sense of the mind is, in part, a matter of modelling, and philosophers and scientists have created an astonishing number of models. Some liken the mind to a computer. Some emphasise symbols and ‘mentalese’, a hypothesised ‘language of thought’. Some start from the brain and its physical, neural basis. These models aren’t necessarily in conflict: for instance, the ‘working memory’ model proposed by the psychologists Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch may complement ‘predictive processing’ models of vision or attention theorised by the computational neuroscientists Rajesh Rao, Dana Ballard and Karl Friston. The domain is crowded, and still growing.

However, nearly all of these models neglect something essential to how the human mind functions: metabolism. They describe what the mind computes, or how its neurons signal, but not the metabolic work by which the brain acquires energy, maintains homeostasis, and disposes of waste. Without taking metabolism into consideration, our models are in danger of becoming untethered from real-world constraints, turning the ancient goal of understanding the mind into a wild goose chase.

So what happens if we take brain metabolism seriously?

‘Metabolism’ refers to activities that all biological systems, the brain included, carry out in order to stay alive. It includes energy use, but also maintenance, regulation and waste removal. Metabolism informs models of how our muscles work when we run, how our lungs work when we breathe, and how our immune system works when we get sick. Since the human mind has something to do with the brain, it stands to reason that metabolism should inform models of how our brain works when we think. And, indeed, most scholars nowadays tend to accept that the brain is important to understanding the mind, even if they leave it out of their models.

The brain is a quirky organ, metabolically speaking. It consumes a lot of energy compared with other parts of the human body. Though it makes up around 2 per cent of an adult’s body mass, it consumes about 20 per cent of its calories. Yet it is impressively efficient. The brain on average operates at about 20 watts – less than an incandescent lightbulb. A ‘lightbulb moment’, in other words, probably consumes less energy than an actual lightbulb.

According to one study by William Levy and Victoria Calvert of the University of Virginia, the electrical signals (or ‘spikes’) that send information use only about 3.5 watts. Building and strengthening synapses, which is how information is stored, uses about 1.3 watts. It is not entirely understood how the brain can do so much with so little, but part of the answer is evolution: organisms with more efficient brains had a selective advantage for searching for food and avoiding predators. The human mind operates under tremendous metabolic constraints.

A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support

Focusing on metabolism might seem to fly in the face of much philosophical analysis of the mind. Many philosophers set the brain aside when building their theories, freeing the mind from its substratum. One reason is the widespread acceptance of multiple realisability, a view first set out by the philosopher Hilary Putnam in the 1960s, which holds that the same mental states can be realised by different neural states. What determines a mental state is what it does, not what it’s made of. This is how an octopus could still feel pain, even if its brain is unlike ours – it’s the state that matters, not the physical substratum. Some philosophers go further, adopting John Haugeland’s notion of ‘medium independence’: if mental states are computations – a mainstream view in cognitive science – then these states are independent of the specific medium in which they are embodied. Mental states are defined by formal rules, and these same rules can be implemented in different media. The familiar analogy is the computer: the same software (the mind) can be run on different hardware (the brain). Both views reject the idea that there is a one-to-one match between the mind and the brain. They suggest that the mind can be fruitfully studied on its own terms, making metabolism irrelevant to modelling.

Yet even brain-friendly philosophers have largely disregarded brain metabolism. Patricia Churchland, who urged philosophers to learn neuroscience, co-wrote a 1988 paper that defined the aim of computational neuroscience as explaining how the brain’s signals are used ‘to represent and process information’. But the chemistry that maintains those signals was lost in this framing. The philosopher Carl Craver and colleagues stay close to the biological ground when they argue that mechanisms are ‘entities and activities organised such that they are productive of regular changes’, for example neurotransmitters binding to receptors. But here too the energy that makes those activities possible figures as a background condition rather than as part of the explanation.

We argue that metabolism constrains which models of the mind are viable. But that does not require the mind to be uniquely realised by the brain: metabolic constraints narrow the options without settling on a single one. Consider the example of memory storage. It could occur via different brain processes, or in nonbiological media like silicon-based digital computers. Whatever the medium, all these systems will be constrained by energy use, maintenance and waste removal. A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support, and studying metabolism is how we find out where that limit lies.…

item.title: Fairuz in the morning and Umm Kulthum at night
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, personal narrative, and cultural insight

Chatter floats around me and smoke rises from the bonfire. It is a warm August night in the Philadelphia suburbs, and one of my friends slowly taps the darbuka under his arm. Then he sings Umm Kulthum’s ‘Alf Leila Wa Leila’ (‘A Thousand and One Nights’). One after another, we join in, singing along to what I once considered the epitome of old people’s music:

My love, my love,

The night and its sky, its stars and its moon, its moon and its awakening,

and you and me, my own love, my own life.

The next line comes to me instinctively. I’m singing in ecstasy, as my parents used to on our night rides. I laugh to myself as I watch my friends sway in their seats.

I’m back at my grandparents’ house in the Palestinian town of Beit Sahour. After playing in their yard until sunset, my cousins and I would gather on their bed, where Teta would turn down Umm Kulthum on the television to tell us the story of the Elderly Woman and her Cow while slicing apples. Now and then, I’d glance at the flickering black-and-white screen to see the audience clap, sway and cry out in a state of tarab, surrendering to what they called ‘her grandeur’. She would finish a stanza, and the audience would erupt in applause, calling out Azama ala azama, ya Sit! (‘Greatness upon greatness, oh lady!’), waiting for her to sing again.

They were out of their minds, I thought. Why such reverence for an Egyptian woman with dark sunglasses, a silk handkerchief draped over her hand, standing on a stage for hours accompanied by a full orchestra, repeating almost the same lyrics relentlessly?

Morning came and so did Fairuz. I woke up to my grandfather’s voice calling me. Eyes half-open, I put on my school uniform and ran down the stairs to my grandparents’ house, the scent of Arabic coffee rising from the stove. My Teta was in the backyard. She embraced me with her flour-dusted hands, then continued kneading the dough, humming along with the voice on the radio:

I write your name, my love, on the old poplar trees.

You write my name on the sand of the road.

Tomorrow winter will come on wounded stories,

your name shall remain, and my name shall be erased.

Fairuz, again. I expressed my dismay at the music choice, only to hear Teta’s monologue on the renowned Lebanese vocalist, the great ‘Bird of the East’, and the horrific possibility of a morning without her songs. I sighed and accepted my fate. I rolled my eyes and tapped my foot, taking a bite of Teta’s bread and waiting to be saved by my ride to school.

Naively, I had forgotten that my suffering would not end. It felt like an epidemic when Fairuz’s voice trailed from Teta’s radio to Amo Essam’s van. Oblivious to my frustration, with a cigarette between his teeth, he would sing along:

The people have asked me about you, my darling.

They’ve written letters and the wind took them.

It’s not easy for me to sing, my darling,

when for the first time, we are not together.

We left Beit Sahour when I was 15 for a ‘better life’, my father said – one where his kids’ futures would not be restricted by political turmoil and economic instability, but filled with security, opportunity and dignity that presumably awaited us in the West. So, in the summer of 2017, we packed our bags, gathering whatever crumbs of our life in Beit Sahour we could carry, and headed for the United States.

Philadelphia was beautiful – tall buildings and ancient architecture, enormous roads, and cheesesteak shops around every other corner. As we explored the suburbs for a place to settle, we drove past rows of identical houses with gable roofs, vast stretches of lawn and fast-food chains. Walmart was a sensational experience. It was our family’s picnic destination for the first few weekends in the US. I couldn’t believe there was a store with gardening tools, clothes, groceries and toys, all under one roof. There seemed to be infinite choices for everything – milk, bread and even eggs: cage-free, organic, conventional, and free-range. I had no clue what any of it meant. It was just eggs.

The mornings were quiet. I started eating a blueberry muffin on my way to school. I sat alone on the bus, where the speakers blasted country music. I had nothing to say to the bus driver. I searched for an English equivalent of Ya’tik Al Afiye. But my tongue was tied, and I settled for ‘Thank you.’

My ears searched for Arabic across campus. Before long, I was surrounded by people who looked and spoke like me

Amid the white American student body, my frizzy hair, bushy brows and distinctive nose made me conspicuous. Although students invited me to join their table, I sometimes chose to eat lunch alone, especially when I had a za’tar mankoushe – flatbread with dried crushed thyme and olive oil. I dreaded explaining that, no, I was not having marijuana for lunch.

I was not necessarily left out – kids liked to sit with me and ask me about my life in Palestine – but I always felt like an exotic creature among them. I couldn’t follow their conversations and cultural references. Listening to Taylor Swift, watching American TV or wearing flannels with miniskirts never quite made me feel that I belonged. Back with my family, I would exhale a long breath of Arabic phrases, exhausted from a seven-hour shift of imitating an American accent.

In college, I gravitated toward Arabs wherever I found them – and I was determined to find them. My ears searched for Arabic across campus, and when I detected it, I was filled with such giddiness that I ran to introduce myself. Before long, I was surrounded by people who looked and spoke like me. For the first time in my life, my closest friends were Jordanian, Lebanese, Syrian and Egyptian. We ate za’tar mankoushe together, argued over who made the best shawarma, laughed at the differences between our accents and traded stories about our homelands.…

Why it is here: original reporting, historical context, and cultural significance

What happened to King Harold's children after the battle of Hastings?

William the Conqueror had conquered and launched a new era in England under the Normans, but he had to keep an eye on the heirs of his fallen foe

The battle of Hastings was over: from the bloody fighting on 14 October 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, emerged as King of England while Harold Godwinson, after less than a year on the throne, was dead.

The Norman Conquest had begun, yet the family of the fallen king still posed a threat to William the Conqueror. Yes, three of Harold’s brothers also died that same year: Tostig had allied with Harald Hardrada and been killed at the battle of Stamford Bridge, while Gyrth and Leofwine perished alongside Harold at Hastings.

But in the early years of William’s reign Harold’s mother Gytha became a figurehead of rebellion in Exeter, and there were concerns that his seven children may one day seek to restore their line.

Who were Harold Godwinson’s children?

Harold Godwinson had five sons and two daughters. With his first wife, Edith Swanneck, he had three boys, Godwin, Edmund and Magnus, and two girls, Gunhild and Gytha. He had two more boys, Harold and Ulf, possibly with his second wife, Ealdgyth, although the lack of historical records means there remains confusion over who gave birth to Ulf.

What happened to Harold’s wives?

Details are scant, but it seems that Edith Swanneck – also called Edith the Fair or the Handfasted Queen as she may have been unofficially married to Harold – survived the immediate aftermath of the battle of Hastings. According to legend, it was she who identified Harold’s body on the battlefield.

Ealdgyth, or Edith of Mercia, was married to Harold in early 1066 as part of a political alliance. After Hastings, her brothers, the earls of Mercia and Northumberland, took her to Chester for safety. It was possibly there that she gave birth to Ulf.

What happened to Harold’s sons?

The eldest sons, Godwin and Edmund, were teenagers in 1066 and fled to Ireland, where they lived under the protection of Diarmait, King of Leinster. Twice, they launched a campaign to western England in the hopes of overthrowing the Norman regime.

In 1068, leading a force of Dublin Norse mercenaries, they failed in their initial aim of seizing Bristol before losing a decisive battle in Somerset. They found no support from their father’s former allies, who had made peace with William. The following years, they returned with a fleet of ships and headed for Exeter, but again failed.

Instead, Godwin and Edmund raided parts of Devon and Cornwall, then, with no hopes of success, they fled again, this time to the court of their relative, Sweyn II of Denmark.

It is possible that their younger brother Magnus accompanied them, but only clues remain in the historical sources. He may have died during Godwin and Edmund’s doomed campaigns, or became a monk in Sussex or a count in modern-day Poland.

Accounts suggest that Harold (junior) found his way to the court of Olaf III of Norway, the son of Harald Hardrada. Despite Harold Godwinson defeating and killing Hardrada, he spared Olaf’s life at Stamford Bridge, so Olaf welcomed the young Harold into his service. It appears that he participated in expeditions to the Orkneys, Hebrides, Isle of Man and Anglesey.

Ulf, however, had been immediately captured after Hastings and was imprisoned in Normandy until William’s death in 1087. By then, any thoughts of opposition had been stamped out: in fact, he became a knight of the new Duke of Normandy.

What happened to Harold’s daughters?

Gunhild was at a nunnery at Wilton Abbey in 1066 and remained in England. She married one of William’s inner circle, Alan the Red, possibly a strategic alliance to help Alan secure his lands, which had belonged to Gunhild’s mother. When he died shortly afterwards, she ended up with his brother, Alan the Black.

Gytha, meanwhile, escaped to Denmark and married Vladimir II Monomakh, ruler of Smolensk and Chernigov and the future Grand Prince of Kiev. They had several children together, with one of them becoming known as Harald; a small way of honouring Gytha’s father, since reclaiming the English crown was out of reach.

Jonny Wilkes is a former staff writer for BBC History Revealed, and he continues to write for both the magazine and HistoryExtra. He has BA in History from the University of York.
